summary.text: Meiosis is a special type of division of germ cells in sexually-reproducing organisms that produces the gametes: sperm or egg cells.
It involves two rounds of division that end in four cells, each with only one copy of each chromosome.
Before the division, genetic material from the paternal and maternal copies of each chromosome is crossed over, creating new combinations on each chromosome.

facts.label: Cells produced
facts.value: Four haploid cells from two rounds of division

facts.label: Human gametes
facts.value: Each human egg or sperm carries 23 chromosomes

facts.label: First described
facts.value: Oscar Hertwig, in sea urchin eggs in 1876

facts.label: Where absent
facts.value: Does not occur in archaea or bacteria

facts.label: Error consequence
facts.value: Errors causing aneuploidy lead to miscarriage and disabilities

items.prompt: Two parents each give one cell to make a child, yet the child does not have double the chromosomes. What explains this?

options.label: Each cell loses half its chromosomes after the two have fused
Mitosis in the egg removes half of the chromosomes afterwards
Meiosis halves the number in sperm and egg, and fertilization restores it
The child's cells copy the chromosomes of only one parent

items.explain: Because meiosis halves the chromosome number, gametes fuse to form a diploid zygote, so successive generations keep the same number.

items.prompt: Two siblings have the same parents but are genetically different. Which part of meiosis helps explain that?

options.label: Crossovers mix maternal and paternal DNA in new combinations
The second division copies each chromosome exactly as it was
DNA replication changes the code before the cell divides
Gametes are chosen for their traits before the first division

items.explain: Recombination can give a chromatid a new combination of maternal and paternal information, producing offspring genetically distinct from either parent.

items.prompt: In the second meiotic division, what gets pulled apart into separate cells?

options.label: Homologous chromosomes, as in the first division
The two nuclei of a newly formed zygote
The paternal and maternal cells themselves
The sister chromatids of each chromosome

items.explain: In the second division the sister chromatids are segregated to separate daughter cells, giving four haploid cells in total.

items.prompt: In a female animal, what typically becomes of the four cells that meiosis produces?

options.label: All four develop into mature eggs
One becomes an egg, and three are discarded as polar bodies
Two become eggs, and two become polar bodies
All four fuse back together into one cell

items.explain: In female animals three of the four meiotic products are typically eliminated as polar bodies, and only one cell develops into an ovum.

items.prompt: A bacterium takes in DNA from another bacterium and recombines it. Which statement is accurate?

options.label: It is meiosis, which is how bacteria reproduce
It is meiosis, but it makes only one haploid cell
It is horizontal gene transfer, not meiosis, which bacteria lack
It is binary fission, which swaps DNA between cells

items.explain: Meiosis does not occur in bacteria, but a sexual-like process called horizontal gene transfer moves DNA from one bacterium to another.

items.prompt: A gamete forms with an abnormal number of chromosomes. Which outcome is linked to errors like this?

options.label: Miscarriage and developmental disabilities
Faster growth through the extra chromosomes
Protection against inherited genetic disease
Production of extra gametes in later generations

items.explain: Errors in meiosis that cause aneuploidy are the leading known cause of miscarriage and the most frequent genetic cause of developmental disabilities.

paragraphs.heading: What meiosis is
paragraphs.text: Meiosis is a special kind of cell division that makes the sex cells, called gametes: sperm and eggs. It takes place in the germ cells of organisms that reproduce sexually. One cell divides twice in a row, in steps named meiosis I and meiosis II. The end result is four cells, and each holds just one copy of every chromosome, a state called haploid.

paragraphs.heading: Why halving matters
paragraphs.text: Halving the chromosomes is what lets sexual reproduction work. At fertilisation an egg and a sperm fuse into a zygote, a single cell holding two copies of every chromosome, one from each parent; a cell with two copies is called diploid. Human body cells, for example, carry 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs. Each egg or sperm carries one set of 23, so the zygote ends up with 46 again. Swinging back and forth between meiosis and fertilisation keeps the chromosome count steady from one generation to the next.

paragraphs.heading: Copying and pairing
paragraphs.text: Before the divisions begin, the cell copies its DNA, so each chromosome becomes two identical strands called sister chromatids, held together. The cell then enters a long stage called meiotic prophase. Here the matching chromosomes from mother and father, called homologs, line up in pairs. They swap pieces of DNA through recombination, a planned process of cutting and repairing the DNA. Some of these swaps leave crossovers, physical links between the pair called chiasmata.

paragraphs.heading: Two divisions
paragraphs.text: In the first division, a structure called the spindle apparatus pulls the members of each homolog pair into separate cells. The cells then divide a second time without copying their DNA again. This time the sister chromatids come apart, much as they do in mitosis, the ordinary division that turns one cell into two identical ones. That leaves four haploid cells in all.

paragraphs.heading: A source of variety
paragraphs.text: Because of recombination, a single chromatid can carry a fresh mix of the mother's and the father's genetic information. On top of that, each gamete gets its own blend of maternal, paternal and mixed chromatids. That is why offspring differ genetically from both parents. This variety feeds the differences in traits that natural selection works on.

paragraphs.heading: Where it happens
paragraphs.text: Meiosis is found in every sexually reproducing organism, single-celled or many-celled, including animals, plants and fungi. In some cases all four products become gametes, spores or pollen. In female animals, though, three of the four are usually cast off as small polar bodies, and only one becomes an egg. Bacteria and archaea do not use meiosis at all.

paragraphs.heading: When it goes wrong
paragraphs.text: Mistakes in meiosis can produce aneuploidy, meaning an abnormal number of chromosomes. These errors are the biggest known reason for miscarriage, and they are the most frequent genetic source of developmental disabilities.

paragraphs.heading: How it was found
paragraphs.text: Oscar Hertwig, a German biologist, first described meiosis in 1876 while studying sea urchin eggs. In 1883 Edouard Van Beneden described it again, this time at the level of chromosomes, in the eggs of the Ascaris roundworm. In 1890 August Weismann explained why it matters: to keep the chromosome number steady, one diploid cell must divide twice to give four haploid cells. In 1911 Thomas Hunt Morgan spotted crossovers in fruit flies, which helped show that traits are carried on chromosomes.
